newsitem.title: USA: NASA says no need to evacuate Mir station.
newsitem.headline: NASA says no need to evacuate Mir station.

text.p: Life on board Russia's Mir space station was returning to normal and there were no plans for the U.S.-Russian crew to leave, NASA officials said on Tuesday.

"Things were rough a couple of weeks ago, but right now they are gradually working back into a fairly nominal situation," said Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's shuttle-Mir programme. There was no need for an evacuation, he added.
Russian ground controllers told reporters earlier on Tuesday that the 11-year-old space outpost may have to be abandoned if problems with its cooling system persist.
Aboard Mir are Russian cosmonauts Vasily Tsibliev and Alexander Lazutkin and U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger.

The crew has spent the past few weeks trying to plug leaks in the station's cooling systems. At least one leak remains and the men are reporting irritation from antifreeze vapour escaping from the system.
Only small amounts of vapour from the toxic ethylene glycol antifreeze were thought to be entering Mir's atmosphere, Culbertson explained.
"They probably get some spillage when they are doing repair work, but it's not like its spouting like a whale," he said.
Although there was no way to accurately measure the levels of ethylene glycol in the atmosphere, Culbertson believed Mir's crew was in no immediate danger.
Corrosion in the pipe work of the ageing space station was thought to be responsible for the coolant leaks that sent temperatures in some Mir compartments soaring as high as 88 degrees (31 Celsius).
The three man crew has dealt with a string of technical problems aboard Mir that began with a brief but serious fire in February.
In recent weeks the cosmonauts successfully repaired the space station's primary oxygen generator and a device for removing carbon dioxide from the air.
Culbertson said he was optimistic the cooperative programme with Russia would continue despite the station's problems. Three more U.S. astronauts are due to make four-month stays on Mir.
The space shuttle Atlantis is due to visit the station in May to pick up Linenger and drop off his replacement.
